An infection is what happens when tiny, harmful living things — too small to see — enter your body, survive there, multiply, and cause harm. These tiny invaders are called pathogens (a word simply meaning "things that cause disease"). Your body is usually a warm, moist, nutrient-rich environment, which makes it an attractive home for these organisms. When they settle in and start reproducing, that process — and its consequences — is what we call an infection.

There are four main types of pathogens responsible for infections:

1. Bacteria
These are single-celled living organisms. Most bacteria in the world are harmless or even helpful, but some are dangerous. A throat infection caused by Streptococcus bacteria (commonly called "strep throat") is a classic example. Bacteria cause infections by releasing toxins (poisons) that damage your body's cells and tissues.

2. Viruses
Viruses are even smaller than bacteria, and they are not even fully "alive" in the traditional sense — they cannot reproduce on their own. Instead, they invade your body's cells and hijack them, forcing the cells to make copies of the virus. The flu, the common cold, COVID-19, and chickenpox are all viral infections.

3. Fungi
Fungi (like molds and yeasts) can also cause infections, usually on or near the skin. Athlete's foot and oral thrush (a white coating in the mouth) are common fungal infections. These tend to thrive in warm, damp places on the body.

4. Parasites
These are organisms that live inside or on a host (you) and feed off it. Malaria, for example, is caused by a microscopic parasite that enters the bloodstream through a mosquito bite. Tapeworms are another example — a larger parasite that can live in the intestines.
How Does an Infection Enter the Body?

Pathogens are not magically inside you — they have to get in somehow. Common entry routes include:

  • Breathing contaminated air (e.g., someone coughs near you and you inhale virus particles)
  • Touching something contaminated and then touching your eyes, nose, or mouth
  • Eating or drinking food or water that carries pathogens
  • A break in the skin — a cut, wound, or insect bite that lets pathogens bypass the skin's protective barrier
  • Direct contact with an infected person (e.g., kissing, sexual contact)

One important distinction to understand is where an infection takes hold:

  • A localized infection is contained in one specific part of the body. An infected cut on your finger, for example, stays near the wound. You'll see redness, swelling, and pus right there at that spot.
  • A systemic infection is one that has spread through the entire body, usually through the bloodstream. This is more serious. The flu, for instance, makes your whole body feel sick — not just your throat — because the virus is circulating widely.
Signs That an Infection Is Happening

When your body detects invaders, your immune system launches a defense. This defense itself produces many of the symptoms you feel. Common signs of infection include:

  • Fever — your body raises its temperature because many pathogens struggle to survive in heat
  • Swelling and redness — your immune system sends extra blood and fighter cells to the infected area
  • Pain — a signal that tissue is being damaged or inflamed
  • Pus — a thick fluid made up of dead white blood cells that fought the infection
  • Fatigue — your body is using enormous energy to fight; it wants you to rest
  • Discharge — fluid leaking from an infected area (e.g., a runny nose, infected wound)

Not all infections cause obvious symptoms. Some infections are asymptomatic, meaning you carry the pathogen and can even pass it to others, but you feel completely fine. This is why infections can spread silently.

A contagious infection (also called communicable) can spread from one person to another — like the flu or chickenpox. A non-contagious infection cannot be passed person-to-person. For example, if you get a skin infection from a dirty wound, no one can "catch" it from you. Tetanus is another example: it's an infection caused by bacteria found in soil, not spread between people.

The type of treatment depends entirely on the type of pathogen:

  • Bacterial infections are treated with antibiotics (medicines that kill or stop the growth of bacteria). It is critical to take the full prescribed course, even if you feel better early, to avoid antibiotic resistance.
  • Viral infections are harder to treat because viruses live inside your own cells. Antiviral medications exist for some viruses (like HIV or the flu), but for many common viral infections, treatment just means resting and managing symptoms while your immune system does the work.
  • Fungal infections are treated with antifungal medications — creams, tablets, or sprays.
  • Parasitic infections are treated with antiparasitic medications, which are specific to the type of parasite involved.
Infection vs. Related Words You Might Confuse

Infection vs. Disease:
An infection is the cause (invasion by a pathogen). A disease is the result (the condition of being harmed). You can have an infection that leads to a disease, but not all diseases come from infections (e.g., heart disease, cancer, or diabetes are not infections).

Infection vs. Contamination:
Contamination means a harmful substance has come into contact with something (your food, a surface, your skin). Infection is the next step — when that harmful thing has actually entered the body and started causing harm inside it. A contaminated wound is not yet infected; it becomes an infection when the bacteria start multiplying in the tissue.

Infection vs. Inflammation:
Inflammation is your body's response to damage or invasion — the redness, swelling, and heat you see. An infection often causes inflammation, but inflammation can also occur without any infection (e.g., a sprained ankle is inflamed but not infected).

Outside of biology, "infection" is also used figuratively in everyday language to describe how something negative spreads from one person or place to another:

  • "His laughter was an infection — everyone in the room started laughing."
  • "The infection of fear spread through the crowd."
  • "Corruption is an infection that spreads through institutions."

In these cases, the word is used as a metaphor, borrowing the idea of something invisible spreading and taking hold, even though no actual pathogen is involved.
The Big Picture in One Sentence

An infection is the harmful invasion and multiplication of a pathogen — a bacterium, virus, fungus, or parasite — inside the body, triggering the body's defensive response and potentially causing illness.
